title: Multiple Inheritance Through Interfaces
summary: Discover how Java achieves multiple capability modeling safely through interfaces without the Diamond Problem or state collisions.
learningObjectives: Understand how interfaces achieve multiple inheritance of type without multiple inheritance of state
Master the syntax of extending one class while implementing multiple interfaces
Learn how interface contracts avoid conflicting field and constructor ambiguities
Preview default method collision resolution in Java 8+
expectedOutcomes: Ability to combine class inheritance with multiple interface implementations in Java
Understanding the clear distinction between class extension and interface implementation

activities.title: The Professional Certifications Analogy
activities.content:
A human can have only **one biological father and mother lineage** (single parent lineage in genealogy).

However, that same individual can hold **multiple legal certifications** simultaneously: a Driver's License, a Commercial Pilot's License, and a Certified Public Accountant (CPA) license.

Each certification is a contract specifying capabilities you must fulfill: a Driver must know how to brake and signal; a Pilot must know how to navigate air traffic. Because certifications do not carry biological DNA (state), you can hold as many certifications as you can fulfill without biological conflict.

In Java, a class can have only one class lineage (`extends`), but can commit to multiple certification contracts (`implements InterfaceA, InterfaceB`).

activities.title: Multiple Inheritance of Type vs Implementation State
activities.content:
Java solves the multiple inheritance dilemma by separating **State Inheritance** from **Behavioral Contracts**.

### 1. The Core Distinction:
- **Class Extension (`extends`)**: Inherits fields (state), constructors, and concrete method implementations. Limited to **at most ONE class**.
- **Interface Implementation (`implements`)**: Inherits purely behavioral contracts (method signatures). A class can implement **unlimited interfaces**.

```java
public class Duck extends Animal implements Flyer, Swimmer {
    // Extends 1 parent class (Animal)
    // Implements 2 interface contracts (Flyer, Swimmer)
}
```

### 2. Why Interfaces Are Safe from State Collisions:
- Interfaces do **NOT have instance variables**. They cannot define non-static fields that cause state duplication in heap objects.
- Interfaces do **NOT have constructors**. They do not introduce complex constructor chaining dependencies.

### 3. Java 8+ Default Methods and Collision Resolution:
- If interface `A` and interface `B` both define a `default void log()` method with the same signature:
- Java forces the implementing class to explicitly override `log()` and specify which version to invoke: `A.super.log();` or `B.super.log();`.
- The compiler strictly prevents runtime ambiguity.

activities.title: Extending a Class While Implementing Multiple Interfaces
activities.description: Observe an AmphibiousVehicle extending Vehicle while fulfilling RoadDriveable and WaterNavigable contracts.

steps.description: Vehicle acts as the single parent class containing the vin field.
RoadDriveable and WaterNavigable define pure behavioral capabilities without instance variables.
AmphibiousCar extends Vehicle and implements both interfaces cleanly.

activities.title: Example 2: Resolving Default Method Collisions Explicitly
activities.description: See how the Java compiler requires explicit resolution when two interfaces provide conflicting default implementations.

steps.description: Both LoggerAlpha and LoggerBeta provide conflicting default logMessage methods.
DualLogger overrides logMessage and explicitly invokes LoggerAlpha.super.logMessage().

activities.title: Mastery Verification: Multiple Inheritance Through Interfaces (10 Questions)

questions.question: How does Java support multiple inheritance?
options: Through multiple class inheritance using commas
Through interfaces (a class can implement multiple interfaces)
Using the multiple keyword
Using nested static classes
questions.explanation: Java supports multiple inheritance of type through interfaces ('implements A, B').

questions.question: Why do interfaces not cause instance variable state collisions in multiple inheritance?
options: Because all interface variables are stored on disk
Because interfaces cannot declare instance variables (only public static final constants)
Because variables in interfaces are automatically merged by the JVM
Because interfaces can only contain integers
questions.explanation: Interfaces contain no instance state. Fields in interfaces are implicitly public static final constants.

questions.question: Can an interface have a constructor in Java?
options: Yes, a default zero-arg constructor
No, interfaces cannot have constructors under any circumstances
Only private constructors
Only in Java 17 and above
questions.explanation: Interfaces cannot be instantiated directly and cannot hold instance state, so they cannot define constructors.

questions.question: What is the correct syntax for a class extending a parent class and implementing two interfaces?
options: class C implements I1, I2 extends P { }
class C extends P implements I1, I2 { }
class C inherits P, I1, I2 { }
class C extends P, I1, I2 { }
questions.explanation: The 'extends' clause must come first, followed by the 'implements' clause: 'class C extends P implements I1, I2'.

questions.question: How many classes can a Java class extend, and how many interfaces can it implement?
options: At most 1 class, at most 1 interface
At most 1 class, unlimited interfaces
Unlimited classes, at most 1 interface
Unlimited classes, unlimited interfaces
questions.explanation: A class can extend at most ONE class, but can implement UNLIMITED interfaces.

questions.question: If interface A and interface B both define an identical default method void reset(), what happens when class C implements both?
options: The program compiles and runs interface A's version by default
The compiler raises an error forcing class C to override reset() and resolve the collision
The JVM picks a random version at runtime
Both methods execute sequentially
questions.explanation: The compiler detects the default method collision and forces the implementing class to explicitly override the method.

questions.question: How can an implementing class explicitly invoke interface A's default method inside its override?
options: super.reset();
A.super.reset();
A::reset();
this.A.reset();
questions.explanation: 'InterfaceName.super.methodName()' is the explicit Java syntax for disambiguating interface default methods.

questions.question: Can an interface extend another interface in Java?
options: No, interfaces can only be implemented
Yes, using the extends keyword ('interface B extends A')
Only if both interfaces are empty
Yes, using the implements keyword
questions.explanation: Interfaces use the 'extends' keyword to inherit from one or more other interfaces ('interface C extends A, B').

questions.question: Can an interface extend multiple interfaces simultaneously?
options: No, only single interface extension is allowed
Yes, an interface can extend multiple interfaces ('interface C extends A, B')
Only in Java 8 and earlier
Only if methods have different names
questions.explanation: Yes! Unlike classes, an interface CAN extend multiple interfaces simultaneously because there is no instance state to collide.

questions.question: What is the key conceptual difference between 'is-a' via class extension versus 'can-do' via interface implementation?
options: There is no difference
Class extension models core identity ('A Dog is a Canine'), while interfaces model capabilities ('A Dog can-do Pet, can-do Track')
Interfaces are only used for mathematical calculations
Class extension runs faster than interfaces in all cases
questions.explanation: Class inheritance models core ontology/identity (IS-A), whereas interfaces model behavioral roles and capabilities (CAN-DO).

activities.title: Interview Essentials: Multiple Inheritance Through Interfaces

interviewQA.question: How does Java support multiple inheritance when it forbids extending multiple classes?
interviewQA.answer: Java distinguishes between multiple inheritance of implementation state and multiple inheritance of type. By allowing a class to extend only one class but implement multiple interfaces, Java gives developers multiple polymorphism capabilities while avoiding state duplication, memory layout conflicts, and constructor ambiguities.

interviewQA.question: Why can an interface extend multiple interfaces, but a class cannot extend multiple classes?
interviewQA.answer: Interfaces do not contain instance variables or constructors. When an interface extends multiple interfaces, it merely combines method contracts without any possibility of conflicting instance state in the heap. Classes contain instance fields and constructors, which would cause severe collision and synchronization issues.

interviewQA.question: Explain how Java 8 default methods handle the Diamond Problem.
interviewQA.answer: If a class implements two interfaces that provide the same default method signature, the Java compiler refuses to guess which implementation to invoke. It issues a compile-time collision error, forcing the developer to override the method in the class and explicitly disambiguate using 'InterfaceName.super.method()'.

interviewQA.question: What is the 'Class Always Wins' rule in Java default method resolution?
interviewQA.answer: If a superclass provides a concrete method implementation with the same signature as a default method from an implemented interface, the superclass method always takes precedence. The interface default method is completely ignored.

interviewQA.question: What is the difference between an IS-A relationship and a CAN-DO relationship?
interviewQA.answer: IS-A represents core class identity (e.g. A Car is an Automobile, a Manager is an Employee). CAN-DO represents behavioral capabilities and roles that diverse, unrelated classes can share (e.g. A Car, a BankTransaction, and a UserAccount can all implement Auditable or Exportable).

interviewQA.question: Can an interface declare fields? What are their modifiers?
interviewQA.answer: Yes, but all fields declared in an interface are implicitly 'public static final' constants. They belong to the interface itself, not to instances of implementing classes, preventing state duplication.

activities.title: Module 5 Lesson 8 Mastery Checkpoint
checklist: I understand the difference between multiple inheritance of state vs type
I know the exact syntax: 'class C extends Super implements I1, I2'
I understand why interfaces cannot have constructors or instance variables
I know that interface fields are implicitly public static final constants
I can resolve default method collisions using 'InterfaceName.super.method()'
I know the 'Class Always Wins' rule for method conflict resolution
I know that an interface can extend multiple interfaces simultaneously
I understand the IS-A (class) vs CAN-DO (interface) architectural pattern
I can implement multiple capability contracts in a single Java class
I can explain this architecture clearly in enterprise placement interviews
